opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the questions I think about most, because data is really the bottleneck in robotics right now. In language models you had the internet: trillions of tokens that humanity had already produced, sitting there waiting to be scraped. Robotics doesn't have that. There's no internet of robot actions. Every trajectory of a robot picking up a cup or folding a towel has to be collected, usually by a person teleoperating the robot, and that's slow, expensive, and hard to scale.

So I think about it as a pyramid. At the bottom you have the huge, cheap data: internet images, video, text. That doesn't tell you how to move a robot arm, but it gives you a lot of world knowledge. It tells you what objects are, how they relate to each other, what people tend to do with them, and some intuitive physics. One of the big lessons of the last few years is that if you build on top of vision-language models, a lot of that knowledge transfers. The robot can generalize to objects or instructions it never saw in its own training data, because the semantic understanding came from the web.

In the middle you have things like human video, simulation, and data from other robot embodiments. Human video is abundant, especially egocentric video of people doing everyday tasks, but there's an embodiment gap: human hands aren't robot grippers. Simulation is scalable, but there's the sim-to-real gap, especially for contact-rich manipulation and deformable objects. Cross-embodiment data, where you pool trajectories from many different robots, has been surprisingly helpful. Models trained on that mix often do better than models trained on one robot's data alone.

At the very top is the scarce, expensive stuff: real-world, on-robot data in the exact embodiment and environment you care about. You still need some of that to ground everything, and I don't think we get around it entirely.

The open question is the ratios, and how far each layer can take you. My intuition is that diversity matters more than raw volume. A thousand hours of the same task in the same lab is worth much less than a smaller amount of data across many environments, objects, lighting conditions, and failure modes. Failures and recoveries are especially valuable. Teleoperated demos tend to be clean and successful, but a robot in the real world needs to know what to do when it drops something.

Longer term, I think the real unlock is getting robots deployed so that they generate their own data, a flywheel where useful-enough robots out in the world collect experience, and you learn from that with some combination of autonomous practice, reinforcement learning, and human correction. That's how you'd eventually get to internet-scale robot data. But you have to cross a usefulness threshold first, so someone is willing to have the robot in their home or warehouse. Getting to that threshold is the chicken-and-egg problem the whole field is working on right now.

r001.rationale: The response says robot trajectories must be collected on robots, usually through slow, expensive teleoperation, which communicates that hardware-dependent collection slows data acquisition.

r002.rationale: It argues that diverse data is more valuable than repeated data, but does not state that repetitive data is insufficient to achieve general intelligence.

r003.rationale: It does not propose planning collection using effective token counts after processing or connect that approach to language-model research.

r004.rationale: It calls simulation scalable and mentions the sim-to-real gap, but does not characterize simulation as converting compute into robotics training data.

r005.rationale: It identifies data ratios as an open question and favors diversity, but does not propose scaling studies to identify collection needs for coverage across capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that robotics is fundamentally data-starved compared to language or vision. Language models got to train on basically the entire internet, trillions of tokens of human output that already existed. Robots don't have that. There's no internet of robot actions sitting around waiting to be scraped. So the first-order question for anyone trying to scale robotics is: where does the data come from, and what does it cost per unit?

I tend to break it into a few buckets. The first is real robot data, where you're actually teleoperating a robot or having it run autonomously and logging the trajectories. That's the highest quality signal because it's exactly in-distribution for the thing you're trying to learn. But it's slow and expensive. You need physical hardware, operators, and time. We saw this with efforts like RT-1 and RT-2 at Google, where collecting on the order of a hundred thousand episodes took a fleet of robots and well over a year. That's a lot of effort for what is, by language model standards, a tiny dataset.

The second bucket is simulation, which is cheap and fast but has the sim-to-real gap. You can generate enormous volumes, but the question is always how much of that transfers. It's gotten much better, especially for locomotion, but for manipulation with contact-rich tasks, deformables, things like that, it's still hard.

The third bucket, and this is the one I find most interesting, is leveraging all the data that isn't robot data at all. Internet-scale vision and language. Human videos. The insight behind something like RT-2 was that you can take a vision-language model that already understands what objects are, what "pick up the thing next to the cup" means, and transfer that semantic knowledge to action. The robot-specific data then only needs to teach the mapping to motor commands, not the entire understanding of the world. That's a huge lever, because it means your scarce robot data goes much further.

And then there's cross-embodiment, which is what Open X-Embodiment was about. If you pool data from many different robots across many labs, you get more diversity than any single lab could collect. The surprising result was that co-training across embodiments actually helped, rather than just confusing the model. So the scaling story for robotics may be less about one company collecting a giant homogeneous dataset and more about aggregating heterogeneous data and getting the model to learn what's shared across bodies.

The honest caveat is we don't yet have clean scaling laws for robotics the way we do for language. We don't know with confidence that if you ten-x the data you get a predictable improvement. Part of why is that the data is so heterogeneous, and part of it is that evaluation is hard. Running a robot through a thousand real-world trials to measure success is itself expensive. So I think about data not just as volume but as the combination of diversity, quality, and how well you can leverage pre-training from modalities where data is abundant. Volume alone, in the wrong distribution, doesn't get you there.

r001.rationale: It says real robot data requires physical hardware, operators, and time, making collection slow and expensive.

r002.rationale: It says volume alone in the wrong distribution is insufficient, but does not discuss repetitive data or say it cannot achieve general intelligence.

r003.rationale: It does not propose planning collection around effective token counts after processing or connect that approach to language-model research.

r004.rationale: It describes simulation as cheap and fast and able to generate large volumes, but does not characterize it as converting compute into training data.

r005.rationale: It notes the lack of clean robotics scaling laws, but does not propose scaling studies to determine what data to collect for capability coverage.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is what kind of data gives a robot the ability to generalize. You can collect a lot of demonstrations of one task in one environment, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the robot will succeed when you change the lighting, the objects, or the layout. So diversity matters alongside volume: different tasks, different environments, and different ways of interacting with objects.

I’d also distinguish between data that teaches you about the world and data that teaches you how to act in it. Images and videos can give you a lot of information about objects and what successful behavior looks like. But there’s still a gap between recognizing an action and knowing what motor commands to execute, what a contact will feel like, or how to recover when something slips. Robot interaction data is particularly valuable for closing that gap.

So I think the path to scale involves combining those sources, then building a loop where you use the robot’s failures to identify what data you need next. The question becomes not just, ‘How many hours have we collected?’ but, ‘What does the next hour teach us that the model doesn’t already know?’

r001.rationale: The response values robot interaction data but does not say that requiring hardware in the loop slows data acquisition.

r002.rationale: It says demonstrations of one task in one environment may not transfer, but does not connect repetitive data quantities to failure to achieve general intelligence.

r003.rationale: It does not propose planning collection by effective token counts after processing or relate that approach to language-model research.

r004.rationale: The response does not characterize simulation as converting compute into robotics training data.

r005.rationale: It proposes using robot failures to guide the next data collection, but does not describe scaling studies to determine data coverage across capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what kind of data lets a robot generalize. You can collect a lot of demonstrations of one task in one environment, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the robot will handle a different object, a different room, or something unexpected happening.

So you want diversity across tasks, environments, objects, and the ways people perform an action. And you need data that connects perception to action. Video can give you a lot of information about the world, but there’s still a gap between seeing someone do something and knowing what commands to send to your own robot to make it happen.

I think the interesting direction is combining those sources: broad visual experience with robot interaction data that grounds it in actions and their consequences. Then the question becomes how efficiently the model can use that robot data. Can experience with one task help it learn another? Can data from one robot help another robot?

Ultimately, I’d look at scaling in terms of generalization, rather than just hours collected. As we add data, are we making the robot useful in situations we didn’t explicitly train for? That’s the capability we want to grow.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robot interaction data but does not say that requiring hardware in the loop slows data acquisition.

r002.rationale: It says many demonstrations of one task may not support generalization to new situations, but does not state that repetitive data is insufficient for achieving general intelligence.

r003.rationale: It does not propose planning collection by effective token counts after processing or connect that approach to language-model research.

r004.rationale: Simulation and converting compute into training data are not mentioned.

r005.rationale: The response advocates diverse data and evaluating scaling through generalization, but does not propose using scaling studies to identify data to collect for coverage across capabilities.
